text:
You can't ignore the history of colonialism when deciding whether museums should return artifacts to their countries of origin.

The artifacts in question were taken forcibly from cultures that had no say in the matter—often through violence or coercion. Museums, by holding onto these relics, are complicit in this legacy.

These artifacts belong to the people who lost them; you can't just dismiss their claim with a wave of your hand. You have to consider the impact on living descendants who still suffer from colonialism's aftermath.

Can we really say that these objects are safe and appreciated here? Are they truly contributing to our understanding of history, or are they simply being used as tourist attractions?

Many argue that removing these artifacts would be a loss for Western knowledge and culture. But what exactly do museums gain by holding onto them? You might be surprised at how little many of these relics actually add to our understanding.

When we take ownership without permission, it's theft. When we profit from that theft, it's exploitation; the museum system is built on this very foundation—without it, they would crumble. The artifacts are a tangible connection to their ancestral heritage; taking them away silences an entire people.

Some critics argue that returning these artifacts would be logistically impossible or too costly. But we can't put a price on justice and cultural sensitivity; what's the cost of respecting another culture?

We must recognize that our past is not just a collection of relics; it's alive with stories and injustices waiting to be acknowledged—acknowledge them, you will come closer to understanding.

You might ask: should we erase history by removing these artifacts? No. Erasure would only perpetuate the trauma inflicted upon colonized peoples. We must face this history head-on and confront our complicity in its legacy; it's time to make things right.
